sources.locator: GNU C Language Introduction and Reference Manual; accessed 2026-07; provisions applicable to while, do and for
sources.claim: C for, while, and do loops repeatedly evaluate defined control expressions, and correct loops maintain an invariant while making progress toward termination.

canonicalExplanation.summary: C has three loops. `for (init; condition; step)` suits **counted** loops. `while (condition)` checks **before** each pass, so it may run zero times: good for **sentinel** and input-driven loops. `do { } while (condition);` checks **after**, so it always runs at least once. Arrays are **zero-based**: an array of `count` elements has indexes `0` to `count - 1`, so the standard loop is `for (size_t i = 0; i < count; i++)`. Writing `<=` reads one element **past the end**, which is undefined behaviour. Every loop needs **progress** toward its condition becoming false, or it never ends.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner sums 5 marks with `for (int i = 0; i <= 5; i++)`. The total is sometimes right, sometimes wildly off, because the loop reads a sixth "mark" from whatever memory follows the array. A zero-based for loop visits indexes 0 through count - 1 using i < count and performs zero iterations when count is zero. In this lesson you'll write and debug counted, sentinel and input-driven loops.


examples.title: Visiting every mark once
examples.situation: A zero-based for loop visits indexes 0 through count - 1 using i < count and performs zero iterations when count is zero.
walkthrough: **A zero-based for loop:** i starts at 0.
**Visits indexes 0 through count - 1 using i < count:** marks[0] to marks[4], each once; total is 40.
**Performs zero iterations when count is zero:** an empty class will give total 0 with no special case.
examples.result: The total is correct every time, and no memory past the array is read.

examples.title: The loop that never ended
examples.situation: `int i = 0; while (i < 10) { printf("%d\n", i); }` prints 0 forever.
walkthrough: The condition depends on i, but i never changes.
No progress toward i < 10 becoming false.
Add i++ inside the loop (or use a for loop).
examples.result: The loop prints 0 to 9 and stops.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: The condition i <= count is the normal way to visit every element of an array with count elements.
misconceptions.correction: Arrays are zero-based, so valid indexes are 0 to count - 1. i <= count visits one extra element past the end, which is undefined behaviour.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening story, where did the sixth "mark" come from?

analogy.example: A loop over an array is like **counting fence posts starting from post 0**. With 5 posts, the last is post 4. Walking to "post 5" means stepping into your neighbour's garden (someone else's memory).
usefulFor: remembering the last post is count - 1
limitations: Real fences have a visible end; C arrays don't warn you.
A sentinel is a flag planted at the last post.

steps.explanation: A zero-based for loop starts at index 0.
It visits indexes 0 through count - 1 using i < count.
The loop ends before reading past the array, and an empty array would run zero times.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing a counted loop. Step 1, Start: i is 0; total is 0. A zero-based for loop starts at index 0. Step 2, Iterate: i is 0..4; total is 40. It visits indexes 0 through count - 1 using i < count. Step 3, Stop: i is 5; condition is false. The loop ends before reading past the array, and an empty array would run zero times.

nearTransfer.prompt: Write three loops: sum an array with for, count values until a 0 sentinel with while (also checking the length), and ask "Again? (y/n)" with do-while. Test each with empty or immediate-stop input.
scaffold: Guard the sentinel loop with j < count too.

farTransfer.prompt: Find the bugs in these loops and fix them: `for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) a[i] = 0;`, `while (x != 10) x += 3;` starting at x = 0, `for (unsigned i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--)`. Explain each bug.
scaffold: The third never ends: unsigned is always >= 0.

remediation.explanation: For every loop state: **the first index, the last index, why it stops, and what happens with zero items.**
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The loop that never ended".

recap.summary: To write correct loops, use for (size_t i = 0; i < count; i++) for zero-based arrays, while for sentinel and input-driven loops that may run zero times, do-while when the body must run at least once, and make sure every pass makes progress toward the condition becoming false.
